note: The Roman emperor Antoninus told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that he wanted two things: for his son Asveirus to rule after him, and for the city of Tiberias to be freed from taxes, but the Senate would grant only one request. Rabbi answered without words: he set one man on another's shoulders, gave the top man a dove, and told the bottom man to tell him to let it fly. Antoninus understood: ask the Senate to make his son king, then have his son free Tiberias. When Antoninus complained that leading Romans were troubling him, Rabbi took him into his garden and each day pulled up a single radish. Antoninus understood: deal with them one at a time. Rabbi used signs because he feared the Romans would hear, even a whisper.
why: The Gemara has said that the Romans will crown a king's son if the king asks, naming Asveirus son of Antoninus; this story shows how that came about.

note: The Roman emperor Antoninus, a friend of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, had a daughter named Gira who had sexual relations outside marriage. Too discreet to say so openly, the two talked in plants whose names made puns. Antoninus sent a rocket plant, hinting that she had strayed; Rabbi sent coriander, hinting that she deserved death; Antoninus sent leeks, meaning he would be cut off if he did that; and Rabbi sent back lettuce, meaning: have mercy on her.
why: It is one of a run of stories about the secret friendship of Antoninus and Rabbi, told just after the Gemara explains why Rabbi always answered the emperor in coded gestures: he feared that powerful Romans would overhear him.

people.name: Antoninus

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi

note: Rabbi Yohanan suffered from tzafdina, a disease of the gums and teeth, and went to a gentile noblewoman known as a healer. She treated him on Thursday and Friday, and he asked what he should do on Shabbat, when he could not come. She made him swear not to reveal her remedy, and he swore: 'To the God of Israel I will not reveal it.' She told him the cure, and the next day he went out and taught it publicly.
why: The Gemara is asking whether a mouth or gum ailment counts as an internal illness, for which Shabbat may be broken to treat it. Rabbi Yohanan's Shabbat treatment is offered as proof, then set aside because tzafdina spreads to the intestines.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, head of the academy in Tiberias.

terms.meaning: A disease of the gums and teeth that the Gemara says begins in the mouth and spreads to the intestines; its sign is bleeding between the teeth.
A Roman noblewoman; here a non-Jewish woman known as a healer.
The Jewish Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday night, when many kinds of work, including preparing most medicines, are forbidden.

note: A non-Jewish slave belonging to Rabbi Levi used to sell hiltit, a pungent spice, and people bought from him because his master was a Sage. When Rabbi Levi died, people came to Rabbi Yohanan and asked whether they could still buy from the slave. He answered that the slave of a haver is like a haver himself, so they could.
why: The mishna forbids eating hiltit from a gentile because it is cut with a knife that may carry non-kosher residue. This case shows when it may be bought anyway, and opens a discussion of trusting the household of a careful observer.

people.name: Rabbi Levi
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, whose slave sold spices.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan

terms.meaning: Asafoetida, a sharp-tasting plant resin used as a spice and medicine. It was sliced with a knife, which raised concern about non-kosher residue.
Literally 'associate': a person who has committed to careful observance of the laws of tithes and ritual purity, and whose food could therefore be trusted.
